topic: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: what the best-hacking-model eval actually measured, and what transfers to your hardware
title: The $4.65 Hacking Crown Doesn't Fit in Your Download
description:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Enclave AI Hacking Race, local LLM hardware.
The benchmark that crowned DeepSeek V4.1 Flash as the best hacking model ran on a served API where nearly every input token was a cache hit billed at a lower price. The open MIT weights really are the same weights you can download tonight, but the serving stack that made the run cheap stays in the cloud.
You'll learn: why the $4.65 sweep was a serving-stack price, what mixture-of-experts sparsity and an 890-byte KV cache actually do for you, and why the public local proof-of-life is a four-unit DGX Spark cluster rather than one GPU.
(Narration is AI-generated.)
hook_candidates: It hacked eleven targets for four dollars.
Four dollars and sixty-five cents bought eleven hacks.
The crown is real. The copy is not.
The brain fits. The bill of health doesn't.
You saw the headline. You missed the receipt.
Everyone read the score. Nobody read the receipt.
Same model, same weights, minus the caching.
narration_full: Four dollars and sixty-five cents bought eleven hacks. It rode on cache the provider billed cheaper. You've got a gaming PC or a Mac, and you're eyeing tonight's download. Here's the belief the headlines planted: the eval crowned the model, so your download is the winner. The contest was real. DeepSeek's agent got source code, a low-privilege account, and one shell. A run only counted when the target executed a command and submitted fresh proof. The leaderboard itself warns it is not a general model ranking. Now read the receipt. Of the two hundred sixty-eight point three million input tokens the provider counted, two hundred sixty-six point two million were cache hits. A cache hit is input the provider already processed once, billed cheaper the second time. Nearly the whole sweep ran on re-reads. That cheapness is a property of the serving stack, the provider's machines remembering the prompt so repeats cost less. Locally you pay in a different currency: memory to hold the weights, seconds to write each word. What does transfer is the brain. The weights ship under an M I T license, free to use, even commercially. It's a mixture of experts, a model that wakes only a slice of itself for each word. Reading feels small. Shelving it does not. The K V cache is the model's running notes, letting it re-read earlier words without recomputing them. Here those notes cost eight hundred ninety bytes per token. This sentence takes more room. At home, the same bill lands on your memory. The honest local rig is not one card. The public proof of life is four D G X Spark boxes wired together, lookup memory parked on disk. The whole weight set must sit somewhere, even the parts that sleep. Your single gaming card cannot shelve it. Here's where the myth still holds: the open weights really are the same weights, nothing about the brain is hidden. What the eval measured was a model plus its serving stack. Your download tonight comes with only the model.

analogy.vehicle: A library where every question consults only a few shelves.
analogy.mapping: The mixture of experts: the full weight set is the whole library that must be shelved in your house, while each word pulls only a thin slice off the shelves, so reading feels small and storage stays huge.
analogy.limit: The picture implies fixed shelves; the router re-picks experts for every single word, and it says nothing about prompt processing, which reads everything at once.

notes_for_review: Number spend: the desk's three are $4.65 (hook, on screen), 266.2M of 268.3M (spoken only, kept off every screen including scene s3), and 890 bytes per token (on screen in s6); note the fixed hook also says 'eleven', so strictly four key numbers appear, which matches the desk's suggested spend plus the mandatory hook. Spoken decimals kept exact ('two hundred sixty-six point two million'), no rounding taken. The '4x DGX Spark' figure is spoken as 'four D G X Spark boxes' and shown as 4x; 77.2 tok/s deliberately left out per the allowed swap since 890 bytes carries the mechanism beat. Enclave's 'not a general ranking' caveat is folded into the myth framing rather than quoted. The single wry beat is 'This sentence takes more room' (s6), on the number, not the viewer. Analogy limit is stated in-script as 'Reading feels small. Shelving it does not.'; the fuller limit lives in the analogy field. Verify TTS reads M I T, K V, and D G X as letters.
